title: Cui Jian, Chinese rock, folk songs, and the Flower Drum Song
summary: Rowe asks about young Chinese music; Jang recalls performing with rock icon Cui Jian, Tiananmen, and the preservation of folk songs.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well last week, timely, there was a couple of Chinese students. I’m not even sure they were teaching assistants, they did an hour program on Chinese popular music. One did something she called Chinese rock & roll. And the other one did, and I wish I had written the word down, there was a term that apparently there’s a popular style that combines almost hip hop, that kind of thing, using traditional Chinese instruments. It was very interesting. And it’s amazing how pervasive Western pop music is now around the world. And I wonder if you’ve been to China and heard what they’re doing now as far as young people’s music?

Well I think perhaps what you’re suggesting is that there is maybe another transformation with the younger generation? I performed with Cui Jian who is the rock icon of China — China’s first rock icon I should say. As a result I had nothing but my name. He expressed © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -7-

the collective feelings of his generation, you know Tiananmen Square was like 1989. And next year will be the 25th anniversary. But Cui Jian expressed the sentiments of those young students at that time, who felt alienated from the cultural revolution. And so the 1980’s was the emergence of rock, but there wasn’t, you know rock represented rebellion, I guess, of the government. And so it was an expression of that but not necessarily — there was a motivation to think of yourself as an artist and trying to develop something with that music, or develop something that’s distinctively either Chinese or distinctively about that individual, or both. You know I actually don’t separate that. So I guess the other part, the earlier question you mentioned about whether the Chinese embrace what I’m offering is that, like I say there’s sort of a compartmentalization to — and sort of the intellectual process too. So that’s why I’m saying that for those who have studied overseas they can develop a broader perspective. And actually to me, you could go back to the students at the May 4, 1990, you know, that movement. And what was very important — you know that was that big ah out of Bejing University — that the students felt it was important to preserve folk songs. And see to me the folk songs were like songs of survival, in much the same way as the African- American spirituals. So the songs of survival have a very soulful feeling. And that’s why I’m drawn to it. I’m just — I mean I’ve accepted the fact that we’re okay — just put something Chinese there, that’s what it is. But the concert we’re going to give for example, this Friday, with Dr. Michael Woods, we, at a rehearsal, talked about the “Flower Drum Song,” which originated in the Ming dynasty when China was very strong and didn’t really need foreign contact. They felt very confident. And there’s a song called the “Flower Drum Song” which is performed by a husband and a wife during times of poverty. They were like street musicians. And the “Flower Drum Song” was a playful exchange of insults because if you do something funny people give you money. And I said it was like the Chinese dozens. And the dozens is also a playful exchange of insults in African-American tradition. So Doc Woods said, your mamma’s so fat, you know, she could not, you know, etcetera, etcetera. Well you’re from my generation, you know, like from “The Jeffersons,” that television show in the 1970’s, when George Jefferson would perform that ritual of the dozens. So then I did my shameless English translation of the “Flower Drum Song,” the wife would say to the husband well you’re no good ‘cause you’re not making any money, you’re not in the magistrate, you’re not in government — well there wasn’t a government — but you’re not making any money. The husband would go back to the wife and say well you’re no good ‘cause you’re ugly because you have big feet — because during the Ming dynasty there was the practice of the unbound feet which would keep women in their place and not to leave the village.
